title: Requiem in D minor
hook: A Requiem with almost no terror in it. Fauré heard death as “a happy deliverance”, and his music ends among the angels.

painting.title: Death and the Maidens
painting.pairingNote: Young women dance and pick flowers in a meadow while Death, his scythe under a slack hand, dozes at the edge of the picture; Fauré’s countryman paints death as Fauré heard it, close by and without terror.

facts: A [[requiem|requiem]] is the Catholic Mass for the dead, named after its first words, “Requiem aeternam” (“eternal rest”). Most composers make its centre the *[[dies-irae|Dies irae]]*, a long poem about the day of judgement, full of trumpets and fire. Fauré leaves it out, keeping only its last, gentle prayer, the Pie Jesu. Instead he adds two texts sung at the graveside: the Libera me and the In paradisum, in which angels lead the dead into paradise.

Fauré was choirmaster at the Madeleine, one of the grandest churches in Paris. A first version in five movements was sung there on 16 January 1888, at the funeral of an architect, Joseph Lesoufaché, with Fauré conducting. Women could not sing in the Madeleine’s choir, so boys sang the high parts; the Pie Jesu was sung by a ten-year-old, Louis Aubert, who later studied composition with Fauré. The priest is said to have told Fauré afterwards that the church did not need “these novelties”.

Fauré added the Offertoire in 1889–90 and brought in a Libera me he had written in 1877. In 1899–1900 the score was enlarged for full orchestra so that it could be performed in concert halls; this version was first heard at the Trocadéro in Paris on 12 July 1900, during the World’s Fair. The 1900 score is the one heard here; nobody knows how much of its orchestration is by Fauré himself.

The Requiem was written for no one in particular: “for pleasure, if I may call it that”, Fauré said. His father had died in 1885 and his mother at the end of 1887, but he never linked the work to them. To an interviewer he explained that someone had called it a lullaby of death, and that this was how he saw death: “as a happy deliverance”. It was sung at his own funeral at the Madeleine in 1924.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a hushed plea for rest (I), a prayer with a baritone at its centre (II), a floating “Holy” (III), a child’s prayer (IV), a lamb, and a light (V), the only fear of judgement (VI), and the angels (VII).

movements.heading: Introït et Kyrie
movements.title: Introït et Kyrie
movements.summary: The choir prays for eternal rest, almost on a single chord. The tempo then eases, and a plain, flowing melody passes from the tenors to the sopranos and on into the Kyrie, the plea for mercy. One brief outburst and one urgent cry stand out against a movement that is mostly very quiet.

mainIdeas.name: The opening
mainIdeas.description: soft, solemn chords for the whole choir, the voices barely moving.

mainIdeas.name: The tenors’ melody
mainIdeas.description: a simple line, close to plainchant, over gently moving strings. It becomes the tune of the Kyrie.

movements.heading: Offertoire
movements.title: Offertoire
movements.summary: The prayer that the souls of the dead may be freed from the pit and the darkness. It begins as a quiet [[canon|canon]] for altos and tenors, one voice shadowing the other. In the middle a baritone sings alone, then the choir returns, and the movement ends on a soft, radiant “Amen” in B major.

mainIdeas.name: The canon
mainIdeas.description: a narrow melody in B minor, sung by the altos and answered a moment later by the tenors.

mainIdeas.name: Hostias
mainIdeas.description: the baritone solo, which begins on a single repeated note.

mainIdeas.name: The Amen
mainIdeas.description: a turn from minor to major at the very end.

movements.heading: Sanctus
movements.title: Sanctus
movements.summary: The song of the angels, “Holy, holy, holy”. Many composers set it with blazing brass; Fauré makes it float. Harp, rippling, and a high violin line above it, while the sopranos and the men answer each other with a three-note phrase. Only the “Hosanna” brings a short burst of horns and full voices.

mainIdeas.name: The three-note phrase
mainIdeas.description: a gentle rise and fall, passed between the sopranos and the men.

mainIdeas.name: The violin line
mainIdeas.description: a slow melody above everything else, often played by a solo violin.

movements.heading: Pie Jesu
movements.title: Pie Jesu
movements.summary: “Gentle Lord Jesus, give them rest; give them everlasting rest.” One line of text, sung three times by a single high voice over soft organ and strings. It is the last verse of the *[[dies-irae|Dies irae]]*, the only part of that poem Fauré kept.

mainIdeas.name: The solo line
mainIdeas.description: simple and slow, close to plainchant, ending each time on a phrase that rocks between two notes.

stops.hear: A single high voice sings a calm, slow phrase

stops.hear: The same words again, the melody reaching a little higher
stops.happening: The second call

stops.hear: The line widens, then settles, rocking between two notes

notice: The voice is never covered: the orchestra only holds soft chords underneath. Listen for how few notes Fauré needs.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: The soloist is a boy treble, Alain Clément, as at the first performances in the Madeleine. In concert halls Fauré himself preferred a woman’s voice for this solo.

movements.heading: Agnus Dei
movements.title: Agnus Dei
movements.summary: “Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, grant them rest.” A long, flowing tune in the strings carries the tenors’ melody. The harmony darkens for a moment, then a soprano note opens into “Lux aeterna”, eternal light. At the end, the chords of the very opening of the Requiem come back, and the Agnus Dei tune closes it in D major.

mainIdeas.name: The string tune
mainIdeas.description: broad and expansive, under and around the tenors.

mainIdeas.name: The tenors’ melody
mainIdeas.description: rising and falling gently, sung twice.

mainIdeas.name: The return
mainIdeas.description: the “Requiem aeternam” chords of the first movement.

movements.heading: Libera me
movements.title: Libera me
movements.summary: “Deliver me, Lord, from eternal death on that dreadful day.” The only place in the work where judgement day is named. A baritone sings over a steady, heartbeat-like rhythm in the low strings; the choir trembles, then breaks out with horns for “Dies illa, dies irae”, “that day, the day of wrath”. Fauré had written this music in 1877, as a separate piece.

mainIdeas.name: The pulse
mainIdeas.description: a soft, regular figure in the basses, like footsteps or a heartbeat, under the baritone’s song.

mainIdeas.name: The baritone’s melody
mainIdeas.description: wide and urgent, with sudden leaps.

mainIdeas.name: The day of wrath
mainIdeas.description: the loudest music in the Requiem, with horn calls.

movements.heading: In paradisum
movements.title: In paradisum
movements.summary: “May the angels lead you into paradise.” Words sung as the body is carried out of the church. The organ plays a light, rippling figure that never stops; above it the sopranos sing a long, rising melody, and the rest of the choir joins only for a few words. The Requiem ends in D major, quietly, high in the air.

mainIdeas.name: The organ’s ripple
mainIdeas.description: a fast, soft [[ostinato|ostinato]] of broken chords, like bells far away.

notice: Notice where the Requiem ends: in D major, the bright twin of the D minor in which it began.

threads.title: No terror
threads.body: Fauré left out the *Dies irae* and kept judgement day for a single passage in the Libera me. Everything else is about rest, light and paradise.

threads.title: From D minor to D major
threads.body: The work opens on hushed D minor chords and ends in D major among the angels; the opening chords come back in the Agnus Dei to mark the way.

threads.title: Church and concert
threads.body: Fauré wrote it for the Madeleine, with boys’ voices and a small orchestra, then saw it grow for the concert hall. Both versions are performed today, and this recording uses the larger one.
